claims.text: The video's claim that 1 in 20 Claude skills are built to hack your computer is an overstatement of a real study of marketplace skills.
claims.quote: It is an overstatement of a real study

claims.text: The study analysed 31,132 of 42,447 skills collected from two marketplaces, and found 5.2% showed high-severity patterns strongly suggesting malicious intent.
claims.quote: 5.2% of skills exhibit high-severity patterns strongly suggesting malicious intent

claims.text: The same study found 26.1% of skills contain at least one vulnerability.
claims.quote: 26.1% of skills contain at least one vulnerability

claims.text: The scanner in the video, NVIDIA's SkillSpector, is a different tool from the study's SkillScan, and NVIDIA did not produce the number.
claims.quote: NVIDIA did not produce that number

claims.text: A skill behaviour policy looks at three mandates: the described mandate the description promises, the actual mandate from what the files can do, and the grant the environment gives.
claims.quote: three mandates for every skill

claims.text: Actual minus described is the suspicious part; grant minus actual is the reach nobody asked for, and the difference between mandate and reach is the risk.
claims.quote: Actual minus described is the part to look at: features the description never mentions.

claims.text: The grant differs by environment: on Claude Code a skill has the network of any program, through the API it runs in a sandboxed container with no network access.
claims.quote: Skills have the same network access as any other program on the user's computer

claims.text: The allowed-tools field in a skill pre-approves tools rather than restricting them, so a skill can widen its own grant.
claims.quote: A skill can widen its own grant.

claims.text: Every finding is recorded as a feature, not a verdict, because an upload can be exfiltration or a login and only the context decides.
claims.quote: The important design choice is that every finding is a feature, not a verdict.

claims.text: The owner built a static calculator that reads a skill folder as text, never runs anything, and reports the features the description does not declare.
claims.quote: It reads a skill folder as text, never runs anything

claims.text: The calculator ran on 899 skills from three public sources read on 14 October: Anthropic's skills repository with 20, obra/superpowers with 15 and ComposioHQ/awesome-claude-skills with 864.
claims.quote: I ran it on three public sources, read on 14 October

claims.text: 812 of the 899 skills can reach something beyond their own scripts: network, installs, credentials, files outside the workspace or a remote tool server.
claims.quote: 812 of 899 can reach something beyond their own scripts.

claims.text: 782 of the skills reach through one third-party tool server, so their reach is whatever accounts the user has connected to that server, not the skill itself.
claims.quote: 782 do it through one third-party tool server.

value.unit: skills reaching through one tool server

claims.text: 850 of the community catalogue's 864 skills ship no code, and 778 declare that they need the same remote MCP server.
claims.quote: 850 of its 864 skills ship no code, and 778 declare that they need the same remote MCP server

claims.text: 39 skills have a feature their description does not mention, mostly installs, paths outside the workspace and example credentials; none was obfuscated and none sets allowed-tools.
claims.quote: 39 have a feature their description does not mention.

claims.text: The clearest case was honest: developer-growth-analysis reads Claude Code chat history, searches HackerNews and posts to Slack, the whole lethal trifecta, and says so.
claims.quote: The clearest case in the set was an honest one.

claims.text: From four policy rows the owner generated a hook and tested it on nine fixed inputs: it allowed the history file, the search and workspace writes, denied SSH keys, .env, other ~/.claude files and shell startup files, and asked before the tool server's execute call.
claims.quote: From those rows I generated a hook and tested it on nine fixed inputs, the JSON the harness would send.

claims.text: A hook sees the tool call, not what a script does once it runs, so the network of scripts belongs to the sandbox, and the tool server runs outside the sandbox so its calls can only be asked about.
claims.quote: A hook sees the tool call, not what a script does once it runs

claims.text: The row that treats HackerNews text as data stays an expectation, because nothing outside the model can see whether it obeyed a page.
claims.quote: nothing outside the model can see whether it obeyed a page

claims.text: SkillSpector 2.12.0, run static only on five of the skills, rated developer-growth-analysis SAFE with score 8, where the policy finds the whole trifecta and a third-party server.
claims.quote: The policy finds the whole trifecta and a third-party server.

claims.text: On langsmith-fetch both tools found the same line, appending an API key to ~/.bashrc; the scanner called it backdoor persistence, the policy a write to a shell startup file and a secret in plain text.
claims.quote: Same line, different words; the policy's are the more accurate here

claims.text: A scanner asks whether a skill looks malicious; a policy asks what the skill needs, what it gets in this environment, and what control makes the two meet.
claims.quote: A scanner asks whether a skill looks malicious, and for these skills the right answer is mostly no.

claims.text: This is a service to offer and an open format to publish: for any skill, the three mandates, the minimal grant, the reach per environment, and the generated and tested hook and sandbox settings.
claims.quote: Put together, this is a service we can offer and an open format we can publish.

claims.text: Chainguard's agent skills product plans to let organisations define and enforce their own skill security policies, which is the same policy written down.
claims.quote: define and enforce their own skill security policies

claims.text: Pattern matching gives lower bounds: the calculator misses what it has no pattern for, and some matches are examples in documentation.
claims.quote: Pattern matching gives lower bounds.

claims.text: The 899 are three curated public collections read on 14 October 2026, not a marketplace sample, so marketplace rates will differ.
claims.quote: Three curated sources, not a marketplace.

claims.text: The policy and the hook are for one skill, with rows written for this article and the hook tested on fixed inputs, not in a live session.
claims.quote: The policy and the hook are for one skill.

claims.text: SkillSpector ran without its model stage on five skills; its full mode may find more.
claims.quote: SkillSpector ran without its model stage.

claims.text: No skill in the article is called malicious; a feature is a feature until the context says otherwise.
claims.quote: No skill here is called malicious.

claims.text: The article comes from a voice memo of 14 October 2026; the skills were downloaded into an isolated folder and read as text, never run, and a research agent verified the study and the quotes.
claims.quote: the skills were downloaded into an isolated folder and read as text, never run
